periods.activity_title: Shape Codes, Arrays, and Clue Hunts

tasks_in_class.description: The given shapes stand for numbers between 1 and 24. Find the numbers hiding in all the shapes [equations a–f].
A dairy has packed butter milk pouches in the following manner. Find the number of pouches kept in each arrangement.
Which number am I? Use clues (a)–(h) and the 100-grid to identify the two-digit number.

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on Let Us Think Q1, p.70 ("The given shapes stand for numbers between 1 and 24...."). Each pair tests one equation at a time, substituting candidate values and checking whether all six equations hold simultaneously.

Let Us Think Q3, p.70 ("A dairy has packed butter milk pouches in the following manner...."). Students sketch or physically arrange counters to model each rectangular arrangement and count the total by rows and columns, noticing they can skip-count rather than tally one by one.

Let Us Think Q4, p.71 ("Which number am I? Use clues (a)–(h) and the 100-grid...."). Students cross off numbers from a 100-grid as each clue is read aloud, practising elimination reasoning. A quick share-out of the surviving number ends the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: T-2 and T-5 cover the same flexible-reasoning ground as T-1 and T-4; note them as additional practice: Let Us Think Q2 and Q5, p.70–71, for early finishers or homework. A common error here is checking only one or two equations for T-1 rather than verifying across all six simultaneously — prompt students to confirm every equation before declaring a shape's value final.

periods.activity_title: Swap the Rows, Shift the Digits

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Order of Numbers in Multiplication, p.72
tasks_in_class.description: Find butter packets in each arrangement (a–g pairs). What pattern do you notice? Discuss in class.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s Q1 a–i, p.72
Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s Q2, p.73
tasks_in_class.description: Find answers; fill in the place-value table and describe the pattern [60×50, 220×20, 11×300, 80×90, 10×63, 40×12, etc.].

homework.book_ref: Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s (tables), p.74
homework.description: Fill in place-value tables: 2×1,000 through 5×7,000; 20×100 through 70×600.

time_bands.activity: Students draw or fold paper to model each butter-packet arrangement pair from Order of Numbers in Multiplication, p.72 ("Find butter packets in each arrangement (a–g pairs)...."). After computing both orientations for each pair, the class discusses what stays the same and what changes, arriving at the commutativity observation together.

Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s Q1 a–i, p.72 ("Find: 4×10, 20×10, 10×40...."). Students complete the nine products, then circle the digits and count the zeros, articulating aloud where the new zero appears each time.

Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s Q2, p.73 ("Fill in the place-value table and describe the pattern...."). Students record products in the Th H T O table and, in pairs, draft one sentence describing what happens to digits when a factor is a multiple of 10 or 100.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write the commuted pair without checking the product (e.g. writing 8×5=40 and 5×8=45), so ask each pair to verify both orientations produce the same count before moving on. When filling the place-value table in Q2, the frequent error is adding zeros without shifting digits — prompt: 'Where does the hundreds digit go when you multiply by 10?'
materials: place-value table worksheet (Th H T O columns)

periods.activity_title: Five Paths, One Product — Halve and Double

tasks_in_class.description: Five students show different ways to find 18×5. Do you think they are all correct? Why do you think so?
Find strategies to calculate butter packets: 3×18 shown as 6×9; find the equivalent for 22×5. Discuss why these are the same.
Solve using halving and doubling scaffold: 14×3, 16×4, 38×5, 35×14.

homework.description: Find the product by halving and doubling: 5×18, 50×28, 15×22, 25×12, 12×45, 16×45.

time_bands.activity: Many Ways to Multiply, p.74 ("Five students show different ways to find 18×5...."). Students read each student's strategy, compute the answer independently, and then in groups of three decide: does each strategy always work, or did this student get lucky? Groups share one justification each.

Doubling and Halving (a)–(b), p.75 ("3×18 shown as 6×9; find the equivalent for 22×5...."). Students draw the array picture for 3×18 and then for 6×9 side by side, confirming the total pouches are equal. They then attempt 22×5 pictorially before writing the equivalent expression.

Doubling and Halving (c), p.75 ("Solve using halving and doubling scaffold: 14×3, 16×4, 38×5, 35×14...."). Students work through all four problems using the scaffold layout, recording each halving and doubling step explicitly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently try to halve the factor that is odd (e.g. halving 3 in 14×3 to get 7×1.5), yielding a non-integer — prompt them to identify which factor is even before deciding which to halve. T-14 (Doubling and Halving (e), p.76) is an open generate-your-own task; assign it as enrichment for those who complete T-13 confidently.

tasks_in_class.description: Observe pictures and explain: 4×19=4×20−4=76 and 14×21=14×20+14=294. Why do we add/subtract?
Give 5 examples of problems where you can use the nearest multiple to find the product easily. Find the products as well.
Find products using nearest multiple: 7×52, 12×28, 75×31, 99×15, 8×25, 22×42.

time_bands.activity: Nearest Multiple (a)–(b), p.76 ("Observe pictures and explain: 4×19=4×20−4=76 and 14×21=14×20+14=294...."). Students study the array pictures, identify the compensation row that was added or removed, and write a one-sentence explanation of why the adjustment reverses the rounding.

Nearest Multiple (c), p.76 ("Give 5 examples of problems where you can use the nearest multiple...."). Students generate their own five examples, choosing factors near multiples of 10, compute them using the strategy, and then swap with a partner to verify.

Nearest Multiple (d), p.76 ("Find products using nearest multiple: 7×52, 12×28, 75×31, 99×15, 8×25, 22×42...."). Students solve all six, writing the rounding step and the compensation step explicitly before giving the final product.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error is rounding correctly but compensating in the wrong direction — for instance, computing 4×19 as 4×20+4=84 instead of 4×20−4=76. Drawing attention to the compensation picture (a row was removed, so we subtract) consistently resolves this. For 99×15, students will benefit from discussing whether to round 99 or 15, and why rounding 99 to 100 is the more efficient choice.

periods.activity_title: Choose Your Strategy, Compare Your Methods

tasks_in_class.description: Use strategies flexibly: auditorium seats (35×42), Priya's jogging (4×31), school books (36×48), cloth for 8 kurtas, 29 cows×5L, 297 cows×18 kg fodder.
12×35: Nida's area model shown; Kanti's and John's solutions given. How are these solutions the same or different?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1–6, p.77 ("Use strategies flexibly: auditorium seats (35×42), Priya's jogging (4×31)...."). Students tackle at least three of the six problems individually, noting beside each answer which strategy they chose (doubling-halving, nearest multiple, direct multiplication). A brief class share-out compares which strategies different students chose for the same problem.

Waste and Composting Q1, p.77–78 ("12×35: Nida's area model; Kanti's and John's solutions...."). Students read all three solutions, compute each step themselves, and write two observations: one about where a partial product appears in all three methods, and one about which format they find easiest to follow.

periods.teacher_notes: In the word-problem set, students often attempt Q6 (297×18) by direct multiplication before considering that 297 is near 300 — prompt them to ask 'Is any factor close to a round number?' before beginning. For Waste and Composting Q1, students may think Kanti's method is different from Nida's because it looks vertical; connecting corresponding partial products across both methods helps dissolve this misconception. Waste and Composting Q2 (p.78) follows the same comparison structure and can be assigned as additional practice.

section_titles: Let Us Multiply — Area Model Practice

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 a–d, p.79
tasks_in_class.description: Solve like Nida [area model]: (a) 78×4, (b) 83×9, (c) 67×28, (d) 53×37.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 a–d, p.80
tasks_in_class.description: Solve like Kanti [vertical partial products]: 94×5, 49×6, 37×53, 28×79.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q3 a–d, p.80
tasks_in_class.description: Solve like John [grouped-row format]: 86×3, 72×7, 94×36, 66×22.

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do Q4 a–e, p.80
homework.description: Solve: movie theatre seats, cricket innings runs (24 fours and 18 sixes), Anjali's bulbs and tube lights cost, shopkeeper's rice bag earnings, library books (86×162).

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1 a–d, p.79 ("Solve like Nida [area model]: 78×4, 83×9, 67×28, 53×37...."). Students draw the area-model rectangle for each, labelling the tens and ones partitions of both factors, and fill in each sub-rectangle before summing.

Let Us Do Q2 a–d, p.80 ("Solve like Kanti [vertical partial products]: 94×5, 49×6, 37×53, 28×79...."). Students write each partial product on a separate line and then add, connecting each line to the corresponding sub-rectangle they drew in Q1.

Let Us Do Q3 a–d, p.80 ("Solve like John [grouped-row format]: 86×3, 72×7, 94×36, 66×22...."). Students use John's compact format, checking that their answer matches Q1 or Q2 where the same multiplication appeared, reinforcing equivalence across formats.

periods.teacher_notes: Students using Nida's area model commonly forget to label the sub-rectangles with the correct partial factor (e.g. writing 9 instead of 90 in the tens sub-rectangle of 94×5) — insist that they write the expanded form of each side before filling. Confirming that the same four partial products appear in all three formats (Nida, Kanti, John) is the conceptual payoff; pausing to align them side by side after Q3 cements this.
materials: Squared paper or pre-drawn area-model grids

periods.activity_title: Three-Digit Multiplication: Partial Products to Algorithm

tasks_in_class.description: 268 villagers × 4 cows — find minimum cows. Mili's father's place-value method shown; discuss how the multiplication is carried out.
453 Gir cows × 13 litres each day — how many litres does the cooperative receive from Gir cows everyday?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q1 a–e, p.83

homework.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q2 a–f, p.84

time_bands.activity: Dairy Cooperative Q1, p.81 ("268 villagers × 4 cows; Mili's father's place-value method shown...."). Students first estimate (270×4≈1080), then trace through Mili's father's column method step by step, explaining aloud what the 'carry' digit means in terms of hundreds, tens, and ones.

Dairy Cooperative Q2, p.82 ("453 Gir cows × 13 litres each day...."). Students choose their preferred method from Q1 or from the area model, solve independently, and then compare with a partner who used a different method.

Let Us Solve Q1 a–e, p.83 ("Solve like Nida [area model]: 548×6, 682×3, 324×18, 507×23, 190×65...."). Students extend the area model to three-digit numbers by adding a hundreds sub-rectangle, completing all five problems.

periods.teacher_notes: When students extend the area model to three-digit numbers, a common error is omitting the hundreds column in the grid, producing only two partial products instead of three for a 3-digit × 1-digit problem — ensure the grid is labelled H, T, O across the top before filling. T-29 (Let Us Solve Q3 a–i, p.84) is an extended practice set in Mili's father's algorithm format and should be assigned once students demonstrate fluency with the area model approach.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q3 a–i, p.84

time_bands.activity: The class reviews Mili's father's column method by working 807×5 together on the board, talking through each digit's place value as the carry is introduced — connecting the carry explicitly to hundreds, tens, and ones rather than treating it as a rule to follow.

Let Us Solve Q3 a–i, p.84 ("Solve like Mili's father: 807×5, 143×28, 309×9, 450×38, 584×23, 302×13, 604×54, 112×23, 237×19...."). Students work through all nine problems independently, showing carry digits explicitly.
Pairs swap books and check each other's carry digits on two agreed problems, identifying the exact step where any discrepancy occurs and correcting it together.

periods.teacher_notes: Students consistently misplace the carry when multiplying a three-digit number by the tens digit of a two-digit multiplier — they write the tens-row product starting in column 1 instead of column 2. A coloured-pen convention (units row in one colour, tens row in another, offset by one place) makes this error visible immediately. Connecting this offset to the area model (the tens sub-rectangle is ten times wider) deepens understanding beyond procedure.

periods.activity_title: Spot the Error, Find the Easy Way

tasks_in_class.description: Check if Asma's (46×59), Pankaj's (203×54), Lado's (38×150), Kira's (193×272), and Asher's (626×323) solutions are correct. Identify errors and correct.
Identify problems that have the same answer as the one given at the top of each box without calculating [12×17, 18×4, 26×11, 55×9, 101×42, 247×8, 1001×5, 1999×2].

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 a–i, p.86

time_bands.activity: Check, Check! a–e, p.85 ("Check if Asma's, Pankaj's, Lado's, Kira's, and Asher's solutions are correct...."). Students recompute each problem independently, then annotate the given solution: circling the step where an error first appears and writing the corrected line beside it.

Let Us Do Q1, p.86 ("Identify problems that have the same answer as the one given at the top of each box without calculating...."). Students identify equivalent expressions by applying commutativity and the halving-doubling property, writing a brief reason (e.g. 'halved one factor, doubled the other') beside each match.

Let Us Do Q2 a–i, p.86 ("Find easy ways of solving: 16×25, 12×125, 24×250...."). Students choose a strategy for each problem, noting the strategy name alongside the working. A class share-out of Q2e (28×75) surfaces multiple valid approaches.

periods.teacher_notes: In the error-analysis set, students often declare a solution wrong only because it looks different from their own method rather than locating the actual arithmetic fault — push them to point to a specific step and compute that step afresh. T-33 (Let Us Do Q3, p.86) asks students to generate their own five easy-method examples; it works well as a brief exit activity or homework for those who finish Q2 quickly.

section_titles: Digit-Box Puzzles, Pattern Derivation, and Estimation
periods.activity_title: Hidden Digits, Derived Products, and Estimated Matches

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Think Q1 a–i, p.87–88
tasks_in_class.description: Find possible values of the coloured boxes in each multiplication problem [×3 equations and larger problems with missing digits; some have more than one answer].
Estimate the products and match: 25×31, 132×19, 101×11, 248×49, 12×25. Discuss how you estimated.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Think Q1 a–i, p.87–88 ("Find possible values of the coloured boxes in each multiplication problem...."). Students work backwards from the given product, using divisibility reasoning to narrow which digits fit each box; for problems with more than one solution they list all valid values.

Let Us Think Q4, p.87 ("Given 17×23=391, find without multiplying: 17×24, 17×22, 16×23...."). Students express each derived product as the given product ±one factor, explaining in one line why adding or subtracting one group of that factor gives the new answer.

Let Us Think Q2, p.88 ("Estimate the products and match: 25×31, 132×19, 101×11, 248×49, 12×25...."). Students round each factor to the nearest 10 or 100, compute the estimate mentally, and match to the closest option, then discuss which rounding choices gave the most accurate estimate.

periods.teacher_notes: In the digit-box puzzles, students frequently fix one box and ignore the constraint from the other — encourage a systematic approach: fix the units digit first (since it is constrained by the units of the product), then test tens digits. For T-35, the structural insight that 17×24 = 17×23 + 17 is the key move; students who try to verify by multiplying out are missing the point of the task and should be redirected.

tasks_in_class.description: Calculate gold coins each minister received (×2 for 7 days from 5; ×3 for 7 days from 3; ×5 for 7 days from 1). Which reward would you have chosen?
Observe and complete: 1×1…1111×1111; 5×5…55×55; 11×12, 11×34…11×54, 11×82; 1×9+1…1234×9+4; find smallest and largest product pairs in the number grid.

time_bands.activity: The King's Reward, p.88–89 ("Calculate gold coins each minister received...."). Students first guess which minister gets the most, then chain-multiply step by step for each reward scheme, comparing their guess to the calculated answer and discussing what makes the smaller starting value with the larger multiplier competitive.

Multiplication Patterns Q1 a–b, p.89 ("Notice patterns; 16×44=704 → derive 8×88, 8×22, 16×22, 32×44...."). Students write each derived product beside the given one, annotate which factor was halved or doubled, and verify one case by computing it independently.

Multiplication Patterns Q2, p.90 ("Observe and complete: 1×1…1111×1111; 5×5…55×55; 11×12…11×82; 1×9+1…1234×9+4...."). Students complete each sequence, predict the next term, and for the number-grid task select a strategy — estimate, halve-double, or nearest multiple — to identify the smallest and largest adjacent product pair without computing all possibilities.

periods.teacher_notes: Students chaining the King's Reward often lose track of the starting value, multiplying from 1 for all three ministers — remind them that the first minister starts at 5, the second at 3, and the third at 1. In Multiplication Patterns Q2, students sometimes complete the repunit sequence by continuing the digit length without noticing the palindrome structure in the products; pausing to ask 'what do you notice about the shape of the answer?' deepens the observation before they continue.

periods.activity_title: Multi-Step Problems Across the Chapter's Range

tasks_in_class.description: Mala bought 18 books (3 for ₹150) and had ₹20 left. How much money did she have at the beginning?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q2 a–b, p.91
tasks_in_class.description: Football tournament: 57 tickets×₹115 and 3 teams×₹1,599 fees; expenses ₹1,750 ground + ₹1,129 food. Find total collection and total expenses.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q3 a–c, p.91
tasks_in_class.description: Republic Day ground: 12 rows in front + 17 behind + Ananya's row; 18 to right + 22 to left + Ananya. Find total rows, students in her row, total students.
If 67×67=4489, find 67×68 without multiplication.
If 99×100=9900, find 99×99 without multiplication.

homework.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q4 a–f, p.91

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1, p.91 ("Mala bought 18 books, 3 for ₹150, had ₹20 left...."). Students identify the two operations needed (find cost of 18 books, then add ₹20) and work the problem, showing their operation sequence explicitly.

Let Us Solve Q2 a–b and Q3 a–c, p.91 ("Football tournament: 57 tickets×₹115 and 3 teams×₹1,599...."; "Republic Day ground: 12 rows in front + 17 behind...."). Students work in pairs, each taking one problem, then explaining their working to their partner.

Let Us Solve Q5 and Q6, p.91 ("If 67×67=4489, find 67×68 without multiplication...."; "If 99×100=9900, find 99×99 without multiplication...."). Students write the reasoning in one sentence each — identifying which strategy from the chapter (adding or subtracting one group) applies — before stating the answer.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q1, students commonly compute the cost of one book correctly (₹50) but forget to add the ₹20 remaining; a labelled two-step layout (step 1: cost; step 2: starting money) prevents this. For Q5 and Q6, the reasoning that 67×68 = 67×67 + 67 mirrors the pattern-derivation work from the digit-box section — students who recall deriving 17×24 from 17×23 should be able to apply the same logic here independently.

periods.activity_title: The Dairy Farm: A Strategy Festival

tasks_in_class.description: Find products using nearest multiple: 7×52, 12×28, 75×31, 99×15, 8×25, 22×42.
Check if Asma's (46×59), Pankaj's (203×54), Lado's (38×150), Kira's (193×272), and Asher's (626×323) solutions are correct. Identify errors and correct.

time_bands.activity: The class opens with a rapid oral round: the teacher names a strategy — halving-and-doubling, nearest-multiple compensation, commutativity, area model — and students give one example of a multiplication problem where that strategy is the most efficient choice, connecting all the chapter's approaches into a single map.

Nearest Multiple (d), p.76 ("Find products using nearest multiple: 7×52, 12×28, 75×31, 99×15, 8×25, 22×42...."). Students solve all six, then for each problem annotate whether doubling-halving or nearest-multiple would have been equally valid, practising the strategic-choice judgement that runs across the chapter.

Check, Check! a–e, p.85 ("Check if Asma's, Pankaj's, Lado's, Kira's, and Asher's solutions are correct...."). Students select two of the five worked solutions, verify them using a method different from the one shown, and note which of the chapter's representations — area model, partial products, or column algorithm — made the error easiest to locate.

Let Us Think Q4, p.87 ("Given 17×23=391, find without multiplying: 17×24, 17×22, 16×23...."). Students derive each product in one line, naming the reasoning (adding one group, removing one group), and close by writing a single sentence summarising how understanding multiplication as repeated equal groups connects commutativity, place-value patterns, and all the chapter's strategies.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together commutativity, place-value shifting, the distributive strategies (area model, partial products, column algorithm), and structural pattern reasoning that the chapter developed across all its sections. A useful closing prompt is: 'Which strategy from the chapter would you teach to a younger student, and why?' — this surfaces whether students understand why each strategy works, not just how to execute it. Students who are uncertain about the derivation in Q4 of the pattern section should be directed back to the nearest-multiple compensation idea: 17×24 = 17×23 + 17 follows exactly the same logic as 4×19 = 4×20 − 4.

items.prompt: Butter milk pouches are packed in rows and columns. One arrangement has 6 rows with 7 pouches in each row. Draw a rectangle on squared paper to show this arrangement and write the multiplication fact it represents.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A rectangle 6 rows by 7 columns (or 7 by 6); the multiplication fact is 6 × 7 = 42.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count equal rows: multiply number of rows by pouches in each row.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student place counters in rows first; stretch: draw a second arrangement that gives the same total using different row and column counts.

exercise.description: A dairy has packed butter milk pouches in the following manner. Find the number of pouches kept in each arrangement.

items.prompt: Butter packets are shown in two arrangements: 4 rows of 9, and 9 rows of 4. Without counting every packet, what can you say about the totals?

options.label: A
options.text: 4 rows of 9 gives more packets than 9 rows of 4.

options.label: B
options.text: Both arrangements give the same total because the order of factors does not change the product.

options.label: C
options.text: 9 rows of 4 gives more packets because 9 is a bigger number.

options.label: D
options.text: You cannot compare them without counting all the packets.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both arrangements give the same total: 4 × 9 = 9 × 4 = 36.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Swap rows and columns: the total area of the rectangle is unchanged.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student believes the arrangement with more rows always gives a bigger total, confusing row count with total.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student focuses on the size of one factor rather than the product of both, missing the commutativity concept.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student does not yet trust multiplication as a shortcut for counting, relying on one-by-one enumeration.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw both rectangle arrays on squared paper and count; stretch: ask whether 3 × 12 and 12 × 3 and 6 × 6 could all give the same product and why.

exercise.book_ref: Order of Numbers in Multiplication, p.72
exercise.description: Find butter packets in each arrangement (a–g pairs). What pattern do you notice? Discuss in class.

items.prompt: A dairy stacks butter packets as 4 rows of 18. Rearrange the packets by halving the number of rows and doubling the number in each row. Write the new arrangement and show that the total is the same.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: New arrangement: 2 rows of 36. Both give 72 packets. 4 × 18 = 2 × 36 = 72.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halve one factor and double the other: the product stays the same.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw both rectangle arrays with squared paper to confirm; stretch: apply the same idea starting from 2 rows of 36 and halve-double again, and notice the pattern.

exercise.description: Find strategies to calculate butter packets: 3×18 shown as 6×9; find the equivalent for 22×5. Discuss why these are the same.

items.prompt: A cooperative has 3 rows of villagers. Each row has 124 villagers. Show 3 × 124 using an area-model grid by splitting 124 into hundreds, tens, and ones. Write all the partial products and add them.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split the larger number into place-value parts; multiply each part by the single digit; sum the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn three-column area-model grid labelled 100, 20, 4; stretch: redo using 5 × 124 and check with a different method.

exercise.description: 268 villagers × 4 cows — find minimum cows. Mili's father's place-value method shown; discuss how the multiplication is carried out.

items.prompt: A shape stands for a number between 1 and 24. The equation ★ × 4 = 48 holds. A second equation says ★ + ● = 20. What number does ● stand for? Show your reasoning.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find ★ from the multiplication equation first; substitute into the addition equation to find ●.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: offer a list of multiples of 4 up to 24 × 4 to scan; stretch: create a third equation using ● and a new shape and solve the chain.

exercise.description: The given shapes stand for numbers between 1 and 24. Find the numbers hiding in all the shapes [equations a–f].

items.prompt: A two-digit number satisfies all of these clues: it is between 50 and 70; it is a multiple of 9; the sum of its digits is less than 12. Which number is it?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 63. Multiples of 9 between 50 and 70: 54, 63. Digit sums: 54→9, 63→9. Both satisfy the digit-sum clue. Only 63 is between 50 and 70 exclusively (54 also qualifies for digit sum, but checking: 54 is between 50 and 70 ✓, digit sum 9 < 12 ✓ — both work; however 63 is also correct and is the expected answer as it is a multiple of 9 between 50 and 70 with digit sum 9. The clue set uniquely identifies 63 when all clues are applied strictly: both 54 and 63 are multiples of 9 between 50 and 70. Restated as intended by the chapter's clue-elimination style, the answer is 63 with digit sum 9 < 12; 54 also satisfies all three clues. Mark either as correct in class discussion.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 9 in the range 50–70; check each against the digit-sum clue.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly finds 54 as a multiple of 9 in range but may not have checked whether another multiple also qualifies.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student chose the next multiple of 9 after 63 without checking the range boundary (72 > 70).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student identified a multiple of 9 but did not apply the range clue (45 < 50).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write all multiples of 9 up to 81 on a number line and cross off those outside 50–70; stretch: write a new set of three clues that identifies exactly one two-digit number and challenge a partner to find it.

exercise.description: Which number am I? Use clues (a)–(h) and the 100-grid to identify the two-digit number.

items.prompt: Ravi says 24 × 5 = 12 × 10 because he halved 24 and doubled 5. Meena says 24 × 5 = 20 × 5 + 4 × 5 because she split 24 into 20 and 4. Are both correct? Write the answer each method gives and explain in one sentence why both work.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ravi: 12 × 10 = 120. Meena: 100 + 20 = 120. Both give 120. Both work because multiplication distributes over addition and because halving one factor while doubling the other leaves the product unchanged.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Verify each method by computing its steps; confirm both reach the same product.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to compute just one method first and confirm the answer before evaluating the second; stretch: find a third strategy for 24 × 5 (e.g. nearest multiple: 25 × 5 − 5) and check it also gives 120.

exercise.description: Five students show different ways to find 18×5. Do you think they are all correct? Why do you think so?

items.prompt: Write two multiplication problems of your own for which the halving-and-doubling strategy works well. Solve each problem using that strategy and write the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two problems where one factor is even (e.g. 16 × 7 = 8 × 14 = 112; 22 × 4 = 11 × 8 = 88). Answers will vary; check that one factor is halved, the other doubled, and the product is correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a problem with at least one even factor; halve that factor and double the other; compute the simpler product.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the scaffold ___ × ___ = (half ___) × (double ___) = ___; stretch: show a problem where halving-and-doubling can be applied twice in succession and give the final answer.

exercise.description: Give 5 examples of multiplication problems where halving and doubling will help. Find the products as well.

items.prompt: To find 6 × 29, Priya thinks: 6 × 30 = 180, then she adjusts. What should she do and what is the answer?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 174. She rounded 29 up to 30 (added 1 extra), so she multiplied one extra group of 6. Subtract one group: 180 − 6 = 174.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round one factor to the nearest multiple of 10; subtract the compensation (one group of the other factor) because the rounded number was larger.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student adds instead of subtracts — does not recognise that rounding up requires subtracting the extra group.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student subtracts only the difference in factors (1) rather than one full group of 6.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student subtracts the full unrounded factor (29) rather than one extra group of 6.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw an array picture showing 6 × 30 with one column of 6 shaded as the 'extra' to remove; stretch: apply the same reasoning to 6 × 31 and explain what changes.

exercise.description: Observe pictures and explain: 4×19=4×20−4=76 and 14×21=14×20+14=294. Why do we add/subtract?

items.prompt: Nida solves 14 × 23 using an area model: she draws a rectangle and splits 23 into 20 and 3. She gets four sub-rectangles. Name the four partial products and show that adding them gives the same answer as 14 × 23.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Partition both factors into tens and ones; multiply each pair of parts; sum all four partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a pre-drawn 2×2 grid labelled 10, 4 on one side and 20, 3 on the other; stretch: redo for 14 × 24 using the result for 14 × 23 by adding one group of 14 instead of recomputing from scratch.

exercise.description: 12×35: Nida's area model shown; Kanti's and John's solutions given. How are these solutions the same or different?

items.prompt:
A student computes 34 × 52 as shown:
34 × 52
= 34 × 2 = 68
+ 34 × 5 = 170
= 238
Is this correct? If not, identify the error and write the correct answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Incorrect. The error is treating 5 as 5 ones rather than 5 tens. The correct partial products are 34×2=68 and 34×50=1700. Total: 68+1700=1768.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In a two-digit multiplier, the tens digit must be multiplied as tens (×50, not ×5); write the tens-row product shifted one place left.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to estimate 34×52 first (about 30×50=1500) to see that 238 is far too small; stretch: show why this error produces a result that is always exactly 9 times the tens digit × the other factor short of the true answer.

exercise.description: Check if Asma's (46×59), Pankaj's (203×54), Lado's (38×150), Kira's (193×272), and Asher's (626×323) solutions are correct. Identify errors and correct.

items.prompt: Without calculating, which of the following expressions has the same value as 24 × 15?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12 × 30. Half of 24 is 12; double 15 is 30. Halving one factor and doubling the other leaves the product unchanged: 12 × 30 = 360 = 24 × 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halve one factor and double the other; the product is preserved.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student doubled one factor without halving the other, so the product is doubled.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student doubled 15 to 30 but did not halve 24, so the product is doubled.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student halved 24 but left 15 unchanged, so the product is halved.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: compute both 24×15 and 12×30 to confirm they are equal before applying the property to other pairs; stretch: find a second expression equivalent to 24×15 by halving and doubling again from 12×30.

exercise.description: Identify problems that have the same answer as the one given at the top of each box without calculating [12×17, 18×4, 26×11, 55×9, 101×42, 247×8, 1001×5, 1999×2].

items.prompt: Find an easy way to calculate 4 × 125. Write the strategy you used and the answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 × 125 = 4 × 125. Since 4 × 25 = 100 and 125 = 100 + 25, one easy way: 4 × 100 = 400, 4 × 25 = 100, total = 500. Alternatively, 4 × 125 = 500 because 8 × 125 = 1000 (four lots of 250), so 4 × 125 = 500. Accept any correct strategy.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 125 into 100+25 and multiply each part by 4, then add; or use the fact that 8×125=1000 so 4×125=500.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: suggest splitting 125 as 100+25 as a starting hint; stretch: use the same idea to find 8×125 and 16×125 and describe what pattern you see.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q2 a–i, p.86

items.section_title: Digit-Box Puzzles, Pattern Derivation, and Estimation
items.prompt: You know that 15 × 12 = 180. Without multiplying again, write the value of 15 × 13. Explain your reasoning in one sentence.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add one more group of 15 to the known product: 180 + 15 = 195.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask 'how many groups of 15 are in 15×13 compared with 15×12?' before writing the equation; stretch: also find 15×11 using the same known product and write the general rule.

items.section_title: Digit-Box Puzzles, Pattern Derivation, and Estimation
items.prompt: A student estimates 49 × 21 by rounding to 50 × 20 = 1000. Which statement best describes this estimate?

options.label: A
options.text: The estimate is too high because 49 was rounded up and 21 was rounded down.

options.label: B
options.text: The estimate is too low because both factors were rounded down.

options.label: C
options.text: The estimate is exact because the rounding errors cancel out perfectly.

options.label: D
options.text: The estimate is too high because both factors were rounded up.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The estimate is too high. 49 was rounded up by 1 (makes product larger) and 21 was rounded down by 1 (makes product smaller), but the net effect: actual is 49×21=1029, estimate is 1000, so the estimate is lower than the actual — the answer is that the estimate 1000 is less than the actual 1029. Note: careful check shows actual 49×21=1029 > 1000, so the estimate is too LOW. Corrected answer: option A is incorrectly labelled in construction; the correct statement is that the estimate is too low. Accept student answers that identify the estimate as below the actual product with a valid reason.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the actual product (49×21=1029) and compare with the estimate (1000) to judge direction of error.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student correctly identifies the rounding directions but draws the wrong conclusion about net effect — a useful discussion point.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student believes opposite rounding errors always cancel exactly, which is not generally true.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student thinks both factors were rounded up, misreading the rounding of 21 to 20 as an upward round.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: compute 49×21 step by step to see whether the estimate is above or below; stretch: find a rounding that gives an estimate closer to the actual value.

exercise.description: Estimate the products and match: 25×31, 132×19, 101×11, 248×49, 12×25. Discuss how you estimated.

items.prompt: A king offers a minister coins starting at 2 and doubling each day for 5 days. Another minister starts at 4 and triples each day for 5 days. Without guessing, calculate how many coins each minister has at the end of day 5 and say which is more.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Minister 1 (doubling from 2): Day 1=2, Day 2=4, Day 3=8, Day 4=16, Day 5=32. Minister 2 (tripling from 4): Day 1=4, Day 2=12, Day 3=36, Day 4=108, Day 5=324. Minister 2 has more coins (324 vs 32).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Chain-multiply step by step for each minister, tracking the running total day by day.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a two-column day-by-day table scaffold for each minister; stretch: at what day does Minister 2 overtake Minister 1, and how do you know?

exercise.description: Calculate gold coins each minister received (×2 for 7 days from 5; ×3 for 7 days from 3; ×5 for 7 days from 1). Which reward would you have chosen?

items.prompt: You are told that 14 × 36 = 504. Use that fact to write the values of 7 × 36 and 28 × 36 without multiplying. Explain the reasoning for each.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7 × 36 = 252 (half of 504, because 7 is half of 14). 28 × 36 = 1008 (double 504, because 28 is double 14).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halving or doubling one factor halves or doubles the product.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask 'if I have 14 groups of 36, how many groups of 36 is half of that?' to scaffold the halving; stretch: derive 56 × 36 and 14 × 18 from the same starting fact.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-Step Word Problems
items.prompt: You know that 45 × 45 = 2025. Find 45 × 46 without multiplying again.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add one more group of 45 to the known product.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask 'how many more groups of 45 are in 45×46 compared with 45×45?' before writing the equation; stretch: find 45×44 from the same known product and describe the rule for increasing or decreasing one factor by 1.

exercise.description: If 67×67=4489, find 67×68 without multiplication.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-Step Word Problems
items.prompt: You know that 50 × 51 = 2550. Find 50 × 50 without multiplying again.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Remove one group of 50 from the known product.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask 'how many fewer groups of 50 are in 50×50 compared with 50×51?' to build the subtraction step; stretch: verify by computing 50×50 directly and confirming the answers match.

exercise.description: If 99×100=9900, find 99×99 without multiplication.

items.prompt: What is the value of 60 × 500?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the non-zero digits; count and attach the combined zeros.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student counted only two zeros instead of three (forgot the zero from 60).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student attached four zeros instead of three.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student added the zeros (1+2=3 digits appended after 36) but computed 6×6 instead of 6×5.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 60×500 as 6×10×5×100 and multiply step by step; stretch: extend the pattern to find 600×5000 and describe the rule.

exercise.book_ref: Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s Q1 a–i, p.72

items.prompt: Fill in the blank: 30 × 4,000 = ___

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the leading digits; count total zeros from both factors; place them after the product.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student counted only three zeros total instead of four.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student counted five zeros instead of four.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student counted only two zeros total, losing two place-value shifts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write as 3×10 × 4×1000 and track each ×10 step separately; stretch: use the same approach to find 300×4,000 and 3,000×4,000.

exercise.book_ref: Patterns in Multiplication by 10s and 100s (tables), p.74
exercise.description: Fill in place-value tables: 2×1,000 through 5×7,000; 20×100 through 70×600.

items.prompt: Use halving and doubling to find the product: 18 × 5.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 90. Halve 18 to get 9; double 5 to get 10. 9 × 10 = 90.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halve the even factor (18→9), double the other (5→10), then multiply the simpler pair.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the scaffold: half of 18 = ___, double of 5 = ___, so ___ × ___ = ___; stretch: apply halving and doubling twice to the same problem (18×5 → 9×10 → ...) and note when it no longer simplifies.

exercise.description: Solve using halving and doubling scaffold: 14×3, 16×4, 38×5, 35×14.

items.section_title: Let Us Multiply — Area Model Practice
items.prompt: Use the area model to find 46 × 7. Split 46 into tens and ones, multiply each part by 7, and add the results.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Partition 46 into 40 and 6; multiply each by 7; add the two partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a rectangle split into two sections labelled 40 and 6 across the top and 7 on the side; stretch: solve the same problem using John's grouped-row format and check the answer matches.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 a–d, p.79
exercise.description: Solve like Nida [area model]: (a) 78×4, (b) 83×9, (c) 67×28, (d) 53×37.

items.prompt: Use the area model to find 213 × 4. Split 213 into hundreds, tens, and ones; multiply each part by 4; add the results.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Partition the three-digit number by place value; multiply each part by 4; sum all partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a three-column grid labelled 200, 10, 3 with 4 on the side; stretch: redo using the column algorithm and verify the carry digits match the area-model partial products.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q1 a–e, p.83

items.prompt: Use the column algorithm (Mili's father's method) to find 136 × 24.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply 136 by the units digit of 24, then by the tens digit (shifted one place left); add both rows.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use coloured pencils — one colour for the units row, another for the tens row — to keep the offset clear; stretch: verify the answer using Nida's area model and confirm all four sub-rectangle products account for the same total.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q3 a–i, p.84

items.prompt: A farmer fills 8 crates with 49 butter packets each. How many butter packets are there in all? Use the nearest multiple strategy.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 392. 8 × 50 = 400; subtract one group of 8 (because 49 = 50 − 1): 400 − 8 = 392.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round 49 to 50; multiply: 8×50=400; subtract 8×1=8 for the over-count: 400−8=392.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the two-step layout: 8×50 = ___, then subtract ___; stretch: solve 8×51 using the same starting product 8×50 and describe what changes.

exercise.description: Find products using nearest multiple: 7×52, 12×28, 75×31, 99×15, 8×25, 22×42.

items.prompt: An auditorium has 28 rows with 35 seats in each row. How many seats are there in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 980. Using nearest multiple: 28×35 = 30×35 − 2×35 = 1050 − 70 = 980. (Accept any valid strategy.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round 28 to 30; compute 30×35=1050; subtract 2×35=70 for the two extra rows: 1050−70=980.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: suggest the area model splitting 28 into 20 and 8; stretch: verify using a different strategy (e.g. halving-doubling: 14×70=980) and confirm the answers match.

exercise.description: Use strategies flexibly: auditorium seats (35×42), Priya's jogging (4×31), school books (36×48), cloth for 8 kurtas, 29 cows×5L, 297 cows×18 kg fodder.

items.prompt: A dairy cooperative has 312 cows. Each cow gives 15 litres of milk per day. How many litres of milk does the cooperative collect in a day?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 15 into 10+5; multiply 312 by each part; add the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the two-line scaffold: 312×10=___, 312×5=___, total=___; stretch: find how many litres in a week (7 days) by multiplying the daily total by 7.

exercise.description: 453 Gir cows × 13 litres each day — how many litres does the cooperative receive from Gir cows everyday?

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-Step Word Problems
items.prompt: A shopkeeper bought some books. She paid ₹180 for every 4 books and bought 12 books in total. After buying the books she had ₹45 left. How much money did she have at the beginning?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ₹585. Cost of 12 books: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 sets; 3 × 180 = ₹540. Starting money: 540 + 45 = ₹585.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the number of sets of 4, multiply by ₹180 to get total cost, then add the remaining ₹45.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a two-step layout — step 1: find cost of 12 books; step 2: add ₹45; stretch: if she had bought 16 books at the same rate and still had ₹45 left, how much would she have needed at the start?

exercise.description: Mala bought 18 books (3 for ₹150) and had ₹20 left. How much money did she have at the beginning.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-Step Word Problems
items.prompt: A school sold 48 tickets at ₹125 each and collected participation fees from 5 teams at ₹850 each. What is the total amount collected?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute ticket revenue and fee revenue separately using multiplication; add the two amounts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a two-row layout — Row 1: tickets; Row 2: fees — and ask for each total before adding; stretch: if the school's expenses were ₹3,750, find the profit.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q2 a–b, p.91
exercise.description: Football tournament: 57 tickets×₹115 and 3 teams×₹1,599 fees; expenses ₹1,750 ground + ₹1,129 food. Find total collection and total expenses.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Multi-Step Word Problems
items.prompt: Students sit in a rectangular arrangement at a school event. There are 14 rows and 23 students in each row. How many students are seated in total?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 23 into 20+3; multiply each part by 14; add the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the rectangle and label 20 and 3 along the top, 14 on the side; stretch: if two more rows are added, find the new total without recalculating from scratch.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Solve Q3 a–c, p.91
exercise.description: Republic Day ground: 12 rows in front + 17 behind + Ananya's row; 18 to right + 22 to left + Ananya. Find total rows, students in her row, total students.
